title: Where Coffee Comes From
summary: Coffee grows in the Bean Belt, between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. Altitude, climate, and soil all shape how the beans taste.

steps.question: In which region of the world does most coffee grow?
steps.explanation: The Bean Belt sits between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn — the ideal warm, humid climate for coffee plants.

steps.question: Which climate do coffee plants thrive in?
options: Warm with rainy and dry seasons
steps.explanation: Coffee plants need warmth, regular rain, and a dry season for harvest. Frost will kill the plant.

steps.instruction: Match each origin region to the flavor it's known for.
Tap coffee's journey in order, from farm to your cup.
items: Brewed at home or in a cafe
steps.explanation: Each step preserves quality and gets coffee closer to its final form — fresh, roasted, and brewed.

steps.question: Why does origin affect flavor so much?
options: Climate, altitude, and soil shape how beans develop
steps.explanation: Together, climate, altitude, and soil — sometimes called terroir — give each origin a distinctive flavor signature.

title: Arabica vs Robusta
summary: The two main coffee species taste very different. Arabica is smooth and complex; Robusta is strong and bitter. Most specialty coffee is Arabica.

steps.question: Which coffee species is typically used in specialty coffee?
steps.explanation: Arabica accounts for about 60% of global production and is prized for its nuanced flavor and lower caffeine.

steps.instruction: Match each coffee species to its key characteristic.
definitions: Grown at altitude, smooth and complex flavor
Grown in lowlands, more caffeine and bitter taste

steps.question: Which species has roughly twice the caffeine?
steps.explanation: Robusta's higher caffeine acts as a natural pest deterrent — part of why it grows easier at low altitude.

steps.instruction: Roughly what share of global coffee is Arabica?
steps.explanation: Arabica makes up about 60% of global coffee — Robusta covers most of the rest.

steps.instruction: Tap from most delicate flavor to most bold.
steps.explanation: Arabicas tend toward delicate, layered flavors; Robustas push bolder, harsher, and more bitter notes.

title: What Green Coffee Is
summary: Before roasting, coffee beans are green. They travel the world in this raw state, preserving their quality for months. Roasting transforms them into the brown beans we brew.

steps.question: Why is coffee exported as green beans rather than roasted?
options: Green beans stay fresh longer during shipping
Roasted beans are too heavy to ship
steps.explanation: Green coffee is stable for months. Roasted coffee goes stale much faster, so roasting happens close to the consumer.

steps.question: What color is unroasted coffee?
steps.explanation: Unroasted beans are pale green or grey-green — the warm brown we know develops during roasting.

steps.instruction: Match each form of coffee to its rough freshness window.
Tap the stages of coffee from farm to brew, in order.
steps.explanation: Each transformation changes how quickly the coffee ages — ground coffee stales fastest.

steps.instruction: Roughly how many months can well-stored green coffee stay fresh?
steps.explanation: With proper storage, green coffee keeps its quality for 6–12 months. After that, it slowly loses character.

title: The Coffee Plant
summary: Coffee starts life on a small tree. White flowers turn into red cherries, and inside each cherry sit the two seeds we know as coffee beans.

steps.question: What part of the coffee plant becomes the bean you brew?
steps.explanation: Coffee 'beans' are actually the seeds inside the cherry-shaped fruit of the coffee plant.

steps.question: How many seeds usually sit inside a coffee cherry?
steps.explanation: Most cherries hold two flat-sided seeds. When one seed develops alone, it forms a rounder 'peaberry'.

steps.instruction: Match each part of the coffee plant to its role.
Tap the life of a coffee cherry in the right order.
steps.explanation: From planting to first harvest takes around 3–4 years — coffee farming is a slow craft.

steps.question: What is a 'peaberry'?
options: A cherry that grew only one seed instead of two
steps.explanation: Peaberries are sometimes sorted out and roasted separately — many drinkers say they taste sweeter.

title: Why Altitude Matters
summary: Coffee grown higher up tends to be denser and more complex. Cooler temperatures slow ripening, which lets sugars and acids develop more fully.

steps.question: What usually happens to coffee quality as altitude increases?
options: It tends to improve — beans become denser and more complex
steps.explanation: Cooler high-altitude temperatures slow cherry maturation, letting flavor compounds build up in the seed.

steps.instruction: Roughly what altitude range produces most specialty coffee?
steps.explanation: Most specialty coffee is grown between 1,200 and 2,200 meters. Above that, frost becomes a real risk.

steps.question: Why does cooler weather help quality?
options: It slows ripening, giving flavor more time to develop
It speeds up ripening to keep flavors bright
It has no effect on flavor
steps.explanation: Slow maturation means the cherry's sugars and acids reach a deeper, more layered profile.

steps.instruction: Match each altitude band to its typical character.
Tap altitude bands from lowest to highest.
steps.explanation: Origins are often labelled by altitude band — 'SHB' or 'SHG' meaning Strictly Hard Bean / Grown.

title: Washed Processing
summary: In washed (wet) processing, the fruit is removed from the coffee seed before drying. This produces clean, bright cups that highlight the bean's origin character.

steps.question: What distinguishes washed processing from natural processing?
options: The fruit is removed before drying
The beans are washed after roasting
steps.explanation: Washed coffees are depulped first — only the seed is dried — resulting in clean flavors with bright acidity.

steps.instruction: Tap the washed processing steps in the correct order.
steps.explanation: Fermentation breaks down the sticky mucilage so it can be washed off cleanly.

steps.instruction: Match each washed-coffee trait to its description.
Roughly how long does the fermentation step take?
steps.explanation: Fermentation usually runs 12–48 hours, depending on climate and the producer's recipe.

steps.question: Which processing method uses the most water?
steps.explanation: Washed processing depends on water for fermentation and cleaning — one reason it's harder to do in dry regions.

title: Natural Processing
summary: Natural (dry) processing dries the whole coffee cherry in the sun for weeks. The fruit's sugars ferment into the bean, creating fruity, wine-like flavors.

steps.question: What flavor profile is natural processing known for?
steps.explanation: Drying the whole cherry lets the fruit's sugars ferment into the bean, producing distinctive fruity and fermented notes.

steps.instruction: Tap the natural processing steps in the correct order.
items: Spread whole cherries to dry in the sun
Turn cherries daily to prevent mold
Hull the dried cherries to extract beans
Sort and bag the green beans
steps.explanation: Natural processing is simple but slow — drying can take 3–6 weeks depending on climate.

steps.instruction: Match each natural-coffee trait to its description.
Roughly how long do cherries dry for natural processing?
steps.explanation: Drying time varies with sun and humidity, but 3–6 weeks is typical.

steps.question: What's the biggest risk of natural processing?
steps.explanation: If cherries don't dry evenly, mold and off-flavors can ruin the lot — careful daily turning protects quality.

title: Honey Processing
summary: Honey processing is a middle path: some fruit mucilage stays on the bean while it dries. The sticky coating earned it the 'honey' name. The result sits between washed clarity and natural fruitiness.

steps.instruction: Slide to show roughly how much fruit honey processing removes, between fully washed (100%) and natural (0%).
steps.explanation: Honey coffees remove 20–60% of the fruit — more than natural, less than washed — for a balance of sweetness and clarity.

steps.question: Why is honey-processed coffee called 'honey'?
options: The sticky mucilage left on the bean resembles honey
The beans smell like honey after roasting
It was invented in a region famous for honey
steps.explanation: The mucilage (fruit flesh) left on the bean is sticky like honey — the name comes from texture, not flavor.

steps.instruction: Match each honey grade to how much mucilage stays on the bean.
Tap the honey processing steps in order.
items: Depulp to remove the outer skin
steps.explanation: Drying with mucilage attached is delicate — beans must be raked often to avoid sticking and mold.

steps.question: Which origin made honey processing famous?
steps.explanation: Costa Rican producers refined honey processing as a middle path between washed and natural styles.

title: Drying Coffee
summary: Drying brings green coffee down to a stable moisture level so it can travel and rest without spoiling. Even, gentle drying is one of the quietest quality steps.

steps.question: What moisture level does green coffee usually dry down to?
steps.explanation: Around 10–12% moisture is the sweet spot — stable enough to ship, moist enough to keep its character.

steps.instruction: Tap the drying workflow in order.
items: Spread beans on a drying surface
steps.explanation: Drying is slow on purpose — fast drying creates uneven moisture and dull cups.

steps.instruction: Match each drying method to its main idea.
definitions: Airflow on all sides for even drying
Large concrete floors warmed by the sun
Heated drums for speed and consistency

steps.instruction: Roughly how many days does sun drying usually take?
steps.explanation: Most sun drying takes 10–25 days. Naturals run longer than washed because they keep the whole cherry on.

steps.question: Why does even drying matter so much?
options: Uneven drying causes off-flavors and mold
It changes the bean color permanently
It has no effect on flavor
steps.explanation: Pockets of wetter beans ferment further or grow mold, which dulls or ruins the final cup.

title: Comparing Processing Methods
summary: Washed, natural, and honey each pull the cup in a different direction. Understanding the trade-offs helps you pick coffees you'll enjoy.

steps.instruction: Match each processing method to the flavor it leans toward.

steps.question: Which method uses the least water?
steps.explanation: Natural processing skips the fermentation tanks entirely — cherries dry whole, with little water needed.

steps.instruction: Tap from most fruit removed before drying to least.
steps.explanation: Washed strips fruit off, natural keeps it all on, honey lands somewhere between.

steps.question: Which method usually highlights the most origin character?
steps.explanation: Without fruit influence, washed cups let the bean's varietal and altitude shine through clearly.

steps.question: Which method depends most on dry sunny weather?
steps.explanation: Drying whole cherries needs lots of sun — wet weather can ruin a natural batch quickly.

title: What Roasting Does
summary: Roasting transforms green coffee with heat. Hundreds of reactions create aroma, color, and flavor. Longer and hotter roasts trade brightness for body.

steps.question: What happens to a coffee bean's acidity as roast level increases?
steps.explanation: Longer roasting breaks down acidic compounds, making darker roasts taste less bright and more bitter.

steps.instruction: Tap the roast stages in the order they happen.
steps.explanation: Drying removes water, browning builds flavor, first crack marks roasted territory, and development locks it in.

steps.instruction: Match each roast stage to what you see or hear.
definitions: Bean turns from green to yellow

steps.instruction: Around what bean temperature does first crack usually occur?
steps.explanation: First crack typically lands around 195–205°C, when steam pressure pops the bean open.

steps.question: Which reaction is most responsible for roasted flavors?
steps.explanation: The Maillard reaction between sugars and amino acids produces the deep, savory aromas of roasted coffee.

title: Light Roast
summary: Light roasts stop close to first crack. They keep the most origin character: floral, fruity, and tea-like notes with high acidity.

steps.question: Which flavor notes are most associated with light roast?
steps.explanation: Light roasts preserve delicate origin flavors — florals, bright fruits, and tea-like notes — that disappear in darker roasts.

steps.instruction: Tap these light-end roast names from lightest to slightly darker.
steps.explanation: Light roasts cover a small range just past first crack — even small changes make a noticeable cup difference.

steps.instruction: Match each light roast trait to its short description.
Roughly how much weight does a bean lose during a light roast?
steps.explanation: Most water evaporates during roasting. Light roasts lose around 12–15% of bean weight.

steps.question: Which brew method usually pairs best with light roast?
steps.explanation: Clean filter brewing shows off the bright, nuanced flavors light roasts are known for.

title: Medium Roast
summary: Medium roasts develop past the first crack into a balance zone. Origin character blends with roast flavors: caramel, nuts, and milk chocolate.

steps.question: What makes medium roast popular for espresso blends?
options: It balances sweetness, body, and moderate acidity
It has the highest caffeine content
It dissolves the fastest in water
It was the original roast style
steps.explanation: Medium roasts offer balance — sweet caramel notes, good body, and enough acidity — making them versatile for many brew methods.

steps.instruction: Match each medium roast flavor cue to its family.
Tap these medium roast labels from lighter to darker.
steps.explanation: Medium roasts cluster around the end of first crack and the start of second crack.

steps.instruction: Roughly how much weight does a medium roast bean lose?
steps.explanation: Medium roasts lose a bit more weight than light — around 14–17% — as more moisture and CO₂ escape.

steps.question: How does a medium-roast bean usually look?
options: Pale green with no roast color
steps.explanation: Medium roasts have a warm brown color and a dry surface — oils only start appearing in darker roasts.

title: Dark Roast
summary: Dark roasts push past the second crack. Oils surface on the bean. Origin character is largely replaced by roast-driven flavors: dark chocolate, smoke, and bittersweet notes.

steps.instruction: Tap the roast levels from lightest to darkest.
steps.explanation: Roast level is a spectrum — light preserves origin, dark amplifies roast character. Most beans hit second crack around 230°C.

steps.question: What visual sign indicates a dark roast?
options: Oily sheen on the bean surface
steps.explanation: Dark roasting pushes oils to the surface, giving beans a glossy, oily appearance — a clear visual marker of roast level.

steps.instruction: Match each dark roast trait to its short description.
Roughly how much weight does a dark roast bean lose?
steps.explanation: Dark roasts can shed 18–22% of bean weight as moisture and gases escape during longer roasting.

steps.question: Which acidity level do dark roasts usually show?
steps.explanation: Heat breaks down acidic compounds, so dark roasts taste smooth and bitter rather than bright.

title: Light vs Dark Side by Side
summary: Light and dark roasts are not better or worse — they highlight very different parts of the coffee. Knowing which is which helps you choose the right beans.

steps.instruction: Match each roast level to a flavor family it shows off.
Tap from shortest roast time to longest.
steps.explanation: Longer time in the roaster pushes the bean further along the roast spectrum.

steps.question: Which roast has slightly more caffeine, scoop for scoop?
steps.explanation: Caffeine is heat stable, but darker beans are less dense — by weight, light roasts edge out slightly.

steps.instruction: Roughly how long does a typical batch roast take from start to drop?
steps.explanation: Most drum roasts run 8–14 minutes. Faster roasts can taste underdeveloped; slower ones risk going stale-tasting.

steps.question: Which roast usually works better for milk-based espresso drinks?
options: Medium-dark — its body cuts through milk
Very light — citrus flavors shine in milk
steps.explanation: Roasts with more body and sweetness punch through steamed milk, which is why classic cappuccinos lean darker.

title: Grind Size Matters
summary: Grind size controls how fast water flows through coffee and how much flavor it extracts. Too fine = over-extracted and bitter. Too coarse = under-extracted and sour.

steps.question: Which grind size is correct for espresso?
steps.explanation: Espresso forces pressurized water through grounds quickly — a fine grind creates the resistance needed for proper extraction.

steps.instruction: Match each brew method to its correct grind size.
Tap brew methods from coarsest grind to finest.
steps.explanation: Shorter brew times need finer particles so water can extract enough flavor before it leaves the coffee.

steps.instruction: Roughly what particle size suits a typical pour-over?
steps.explanation: Medium pour-over grind sits around 600–800 microns. Espresso is far finer; French press far coarser.

steps.question: Your coffee tastes weak and sour. What's the most likely grind issue?
steps.explanation: Coarse grinds let water rush through too quickly to fully extract — leaving sour, hollow flavors.

title: Water Temperature
summary: Water that is too hot scorches coffee; too cool and it under-extracts. The ideal range for most filter coffee is 90–96°C. Espresso typically brews at 88–94°C.

steps.instruction: Set the ideal water temperature for pour-over filter coffee.
steps.explanation: 90–96°C extracts balanced flavors from most coffees without scalding the grounds.

steps.question: What happens if you brew coffee with boiling water (100°C)?
options: Coffee can taste harsh and over-extracted
steps.explanation: Boiling water extracts bitter compounds too aggressively. Dropping to 90–96°C gives a more balanced cup.

steps.instruction: Tap brew methods from coldest water to hottest.
steps.explanation: Cold brew extracts slowly at room or fridge temperatures, while pressurized espresso uses hot water but a very short contact time.

steps.instruction: Match each brew method to its rough water temperature.

steps.question: If your kettle has just boiled, what's a simple way to reach ~93°C?
options: Wait about 30 seconds with the lid off
Add cold milk to the water
steps.explanation: Water cools quickly off the boil — about 30 seconds gets a typical kettle into the 92–94°C range.

title: Brew Ratio
summary: Brew ratio is the weight of coffee to the weight of water. A 1:15 ratio means 1g of coffee per 15g of water. Stronger cups use less water; lighter cups use more.

steps.question: If you use 20g of coffee and want a 1:15 ratio, how much water do you need?
steps.explanation: 20g × 15 = 300g of water. Ratios scale linearly — coffee weight times the ratio multiplier.

steps.instruction: Pick a typical filter brew ratio number (1 : ?).
steps.explanation: Most filter recipes hover between 1:14 and 1:18. Lower numbers brew stronger cups.

steps.instruction: Match each brew style to a typical ratio.
Tap ratios from strongest cup to weakest.
steps.explanation: Smaller ratio numbers concentrate more coffee in less water — bigger numbers stretch it out.

steps.question: If you double both the coffee and the water, what happens to strength?
options: It stays the same — the ratio didn't change
steps.explanation: Strength is set by the ratio, not the total volume. Doubling both keeps a cup tasting the same.

title: Extraction Explained
summary: Extraction is how much of the coffee's soluble compounds dissolve into your water. The sweet spot is 18–22% yield. Under = sour. Over = bitter.

steps.question: Your coffee tastes sour and weak. Which extraction problem is most likely?
steps.explanation: Sour and hollow flavors signal under-extraction — not enough solubles dissolved. Grind finer or brew longer to fix it.

steps.instruction: Match each taste symptom to its extraction cause.
Pick the target extraction yield (% of coffee dissolved).
steps.explanation: The classic SCA sweet spot is 18–22% — outside that, cups tend to taste sour or bitter.

steps.instruction: Tap extraction levers from biggest impact to subtler tweaks.
steps.explanation: Grind size and time are the strongest levers; temperature and ratio fine-tune the result.

steps.question: Which flavor family extracts last during a brew?
steps.explanation: Acids dissolve first, sweetness next, and bitter compounds late — over-brewing pulls out too many bitters.

title: Choosing a Filter
summary: Filters quietly shape your cup. Paper traps oils for a cleaner taste; metal lets them through for fuller body. Each style has its own use.

steps.question: What is a paper filter mainly known for doing to the cup?
options: Removing oils for a cleaner, lighter cup
steps.explanation: Paper traps coffee oils (and most fines), producing a cleaner-tasting cup that highlights clarity over body.

steps.instruction: Match each filter type to the body it tends to produce.
Tap the steps for rinsing a paper filter before brewing.
steps.explanation: Rinsing removes any papery taste and warms the brewer at the same time.

steps.instruction: How much rinse water is usually enough for one paper filter?
steps.explanation: A short 50–200 ml rinse is plenty — just enough to soak the paper and warm the equipment.

steps.question: Why do many brewers prefer paper to metal for delicate light roasts?
options: Paper highlights bright, complex flavors by removing oils and fines
steps.explanation: Subtle flavor notes show through better in a clean cup, so light, complex coffees often shine through paper.

title: Acidity, Body, Sweetness
summary: Three sensory axes define coffee flavor. Acidity is brightness. Body is weight in the mouth. Sweetness balances both.

steps.instruction: Match each sensory term to its best description.
definitions: Brightness or tartness in the cup
Weight and texture on the palate
Natural sugar notes that balance the cup

steps.question: A light roast Ethiopian coffee is 'tea-like with high acidity'. What does that tell you about its body?
steps.explanation: Tea-like describes a light, delicate texture — typical of light roasts and washed Ethiopian coffees.

steps.instruction: Tap drinks from lightest body to fullest body.
steps.explanation: Filters and grind size both shape body — espresso ends up heaviest because all the solubles stay in the cup.

steps.instruction: At what temperature do tasters often evaluate acidity?
steps.explanation: Acidity becomes easier to read as the coffee cools into a sip-friendly 55–70°C range.

steps.question: Which descriptor is most likely paired with high acidity?
steps.explanation: Acidity often shows up as citrusy or crisp-fruit notes — the same brightness you feel in a squeeze of lemon.

title: How to Taste Coffee
summary: Intentional tasting — called cupping in the industry — slurps coffee across the palate, then notes what you perceive. Temperature matters: flavors shift as coffee cools.

steps.question: Why do professional tasters slurp coffee loudly when cupping?
options: To spray coffee across the palate for a fuller tasting experience
It is a sign of respect in coffee culture
Slurping releases hidden flavors through fermentation
steps.explanation: Slurping aerates the liquid and sprays it over more taste receptors — the same reason wine tasters 'chew' their sips.

steps.instruction: Tap the cupping protocol steps in order.
steps.explanation: Each step reveals a different layer — dry aroma, wet aroma, broken-crust aroma, and finally the taste itself.

steps.instruction: Match each cupping stage to what tasters focus on.
definitions: Released aromas at the broken crust

steps.instruction: At what temperature do tasters usually take the first slurp?
steps.explanation: Too hot scalds the palate; tasters often wait until coffee dips to around 50–65°C for the first read.

steps.question: Why taste a coffee at several temperatures?
options: Flavors shift as coffee cools, revealing different notes
Cold coffee always tastes the same
steps.explanation: Subtle sweetness and aromatic complexity often only show up as the cup approaches room temperature.

title: Common Flavor Descriptors
summary: The Specialty Coffee Association's flavor wheel gives tasters a shared vocabulary. The same word means the same thing at any cafe worldwide.

steps.instruction: Tap these flavor families from most delicate to most bold.
steps.explanation: Delicate florals appear in light roasts; bold smoky notes develop in very dark roasts. This progression roughly mirrors roast level.

steps.question: A coffee is described as 'jasmine and peach'. What roast level is it most likely?
steps.explanation: Delicate floral and stone-fruit descriptors survive only at light roast levels — they're among the first to disappear with heat.

steps.instruction: Match each descriptor to its flavor family.
Roughly how many primary flavor families does the SCA wheel use?
steps.explanation: The SCA flavor wheel groups descriptors into nine primary families — from floral to roasted.

steps.question: What's the point of a shared flavor vocabulary?
options: Two tasters anywhere can mean the same thing by the same word
It replaces actually tasting the coffee
steps.explanation: Shared language lets producers, roasters, and drinkers talk about the same notes consistently across the supply chain.

title: Cupping Basics
summary: Cupping is the standard way the coffee world tastes side by side. A simple recipe, a quiet table, and a curious nose.

steps.question: What is cupping for?
options: Sensory evaluation and comparison of coffees
steps.explanation: Cupping is how roasters, buyers, and judges compare coffees on the same playing field.

steps.instruction: Tap the cupping steps in order.
steps.explanation: A clean, repeatable order keeps every cup of coffee on the table truly comparable.

steps.instruction: Match each cupping tool to its purpose.
Roughly what SCA score must a coffee reach to be called 'specialty'?
steps.explanation: Coffees scoring 80 or above on the SCA's 100-point scale are considered specialty grade.

steps.question: Which ratio is typical for a cupping bowl?
options: About 8.25 g of coffee per 150 ml of water
1 g of coffee per 1 liter of water
50 g of coffee per 50 ml of water
steps.explanation: The SCA cupping protocol calls for 8.25 g of coffee in 150 ml of water — close to a 1:18 ratio.

title: Aroma vs Flavor
summary: Most of what we call flavor is actually aroma. Smell is doing the heavy lifting whenever you taste a great cup.

steps.question: What's the difference between aroma and flavor?
options: Aroma is smell; flavor combines taste and smell
They mean exactly the same thing
Aroma is only for cold coffee
Flavor is only for hot coffee
steps.explanation: Your tongue detects basic tastes, but your nose adds the rich complexity we call flavor.

steps.instruction: Tap the aroma stages of a cup in the order tasters evaluate them.
steps.explanation: Each pass reveals a different aromatic layer — dry, wet, broken, and cooled.

steps.instruction: Match each aroma to its family.
Roughly what share of 'flavor' actually comes from aroma?
steps.explanation: Studies suggest 70–90% of what we perceive as flavor comes from aroma. Pinch your nose and a cup goes flat.

steps.question: What's the simplest way to preserve coffee's aroma?
steps.explanation: Most of what we taste arrives through the nose.
